mappings.note: Element X with six valence electrons forming X2, then a molecule with Y - all four parts are covalent formation mechanism, LO-40. The configurations are given, so no valency is derived (LO-41) and no formula convention is used (LO-42).

The student must total 2x(+3) against 3x(-2) and check neutrality - LO-41's 'calculate the charge on an ion' used as charge balance. Not LO-42: the formulae are supplied in the options, so nothing is written by crossover.

Four statements to correct, each a species confusion: elements versus compounds, molecules of an element versus of a compound, atom counts. LO-39's differentiation list names atoms/molecules and elements/compounds explicitly, which no other outcome does.

Aluminium nitrate, calcium oxide, ferric oxide from names alone - valency recall into written formulae, LO-42. One of them needs a bracket, but the item does not ask why, so it stays a straight formula-writing task.
Four ion pairs to formulae, including a bracketed carbonate and an ammonium cation. Same outcome as the other criss-cross items and honestly so: LO-42 is the frame's single formula-writing outcome.

Choosing the diagram for Cl- means deriving 2,8,7 from Z=17 and adding the gained electron - LO-41's 'valency from the atomic number' and 'charge on an ion'. Not LO-40: no bond is formed, only an ion is identified.

Three formula unit masses (LO-41), but each compound is introduced by a beneficial use - nitrogen fertiliser, phosphate fertiliser, an antacid - which is LO-44's 'beneficial applications' clause carrying real weight in the stem rather than decoration.

Formulae predicted from element pairs, so the valencies must be recalled before crossing over. Still LO-42; the extra step does not reach LO-41, whose valency clause is tied to reading it off an atomic number.

A four-by-three grid of cations against anions, twelve formulae including three bracketed ones. Pure LO-42. Considered and rejected LO-46: the item is a table exercise, not the design of an educational game, which is what LO-46 actually asks for.

Measured masses from the textbook's sodium carbonate/acetic acid activity, checked against the law. This is the 'observe and verify the law of conservation of mass' clause fused onto LO-39, not LO-40, which explains why the law holds rather than checking a set of readings.

11 protons against 10 electrons gives the charge, and the proton count gives the atomic number - LO-41's ion-charge clause throughout. LO-39 would need the item to contrast a cation with an anion; here only one species is analysed.

Deciding ionic versus covalent from two non-metal configurations and explaining by sharing is LO-40; predicting the resulting formula is LO-42. The reactivity comparison rides on the same configurations and adds no third outcome.

The assertion/reason turns on conductivity differing between solid and molten copper sulfate - an ionic compound identified by its characteristics, LO-39. Not LO-40: the bond is never formed in the item, only its consequences are read.

Electron counts for Al, Br- and Hg2+ come straight from the charge; neutrons from mass number minus protons. LO-41's ion-charge clause is the graded skill; no differentiation of species types is asked, so LO-39 stays out.

An activity is described (salt dissolved, solution weighed) and the student states what is observed about mass - the 'plan and demonstrate activities to observe and verify' clause of LO-39. Worth flagging: every conservation outcome in this frame says 'chemical reaction', and this is a physical change, so the fit is good on the verb and loose on the scope.

The balance reading drops and the student must say why the law is not broken. LO-49 is the apparent-violation outcome; sibling item 2bc80e65 uses the same chemistry but asks for the closed-system procedure instead, and goes to LO-39.

List-I ionic/covalent matched to melting point and solubility profiles in List-II. This is exactly LO-39's differentiation of ionic and covalent compounds by properties, with no formation, calculation or formula anywhere in the item.

Five procedural steps of the balloon-and-flask activity put in order - the clearest use in the chapter of the 'plan and demonstrate activities to observe and verify the law of conservation of mass' clause fused onto LO-39. Not LO-49: no violation is alleged, the system is sealed by design.
Criss-crossing 3 and 2 for aluminium sulfate, bracket included. LO-42's valency-to-formula clause; the diagram supplies the valencies so nothing is derived (LO-41).

Pure familiarity-level recall - Lavoisier, 1789, the law by name. LO-48 sits under C7.1, which explicitly spans 'mere familiarity', and that is all this item tests. LO-40 would require the law to be explained or applied, which it is not. Flagged mildly: the frame has no history-of-science outcome below case-study level (C5.2).

The interesting case: an open flask where mass is nevertheless conserved because the reaction evolves no gas. That is the boundary of LO-49's question about changes that appear not to obey the law, and it is what separates this item from the baking-soda ones.

Solve the mass balance for the unknown product mass in a closed reaction - verification arithmetic on the activity's readings, LO-39's fused clause. Its long-answer twin fe7c301a is mapped the same way.

Three procedural claims about the barium chloride verification - keeping both flasks on the balance, whether an open system is allowed, whether a precipitate appears. All method and observation, so LO-39's activity clause rather than LO-49.

Three setups, one of which loses mass, and the student must reject 'the law only applies to closed systems'. The apparent-violation reasoning is LO-49; reading the tabulated before/after masses is the observe-and-verify half of LO-39.
Two balances differing only in whether the flask is open - again the apparent violation and its resolution, LO-49. No procedure is designed and no arithmetic is done, which keeps LO-39 out.
